name: Local or Remote: the ARP Decision
brief:
Every packet a host sends starts with one question: is this destination on my network or somewhere else? The answer decides who the host ARPs for, and getting this straight is what makes the rest of routing make sense.

A second PC has been added to LAN 10 so you can compare a local target with a remote one.
watchFor: Compare the two ARP caches carefully. A remote destination never appears in the cache of the sending host.

tasks.text: On PC1, clear the ARP cache with arp -d so you start clean.
Ping PC3 at 192.168.10.30 — a destination on the same subnet.
Run arp -a and confirm PC1 now has an entry for 192.168.10.30 itself.
tasks.hint: Local destination, so PC1 asks for the destination hardware address directly.

tasks.text: Now ping PC2 at 192.168.20.20 — a destination on a different subnet.
Confirm PC1 has an ARP entry for the gateway 192.168.10.1.
Confirm PC1 has NO ARP entry for 192.168.20.20.
tasks.hint: This is the whole lesson. PC1 never needs the far host hardware address, because the far host is not on its wire.

tasks.text: On R1, run show arp and find the entry it built for PC1.
tasks.hint: ARP is a two-way exchange, so both ends end up with an entry.

extension: Give PC1 a /16 mask instead of /24 and ping 192.168.20.20 again. Predict what PC1 will ARP for, and what the ping will do. Then run it.
debrief:
Host forwarding logic in one line: AND the destination against my own mask, compare it to my own network, and ARP for either the destination or the gateway depending on the answer.

That is why a wrong subnet mask is such a nasty fault. The host makes the wrong local-or-remote decision, ARPs for a device that is not on the wire, and times out with no error that mentions masks at all.
